answer: I'd like to talk about something I did for my father, who has always put his family first. A time I went out of my way to make someone happy was when I organised a small surprise for him on his retirement last year. He had run a small business for over thirty years, often putting the family's needs before his own, so I wanted to do something meaningful. He is quite a modest man, and I knew he would never ask for any kind of celebration himself. With help from my mother and sisters, I secretly gathered old friends, relatives and a few of his long-time customers, and arranged a modest gathering at home to honour him. My mother cooked his favourite dishes, and my younger sister made a small album of old photos from his shop. The look of genuine surprise and joy on his face was absolutely [[priceless]]. He was clearly [[touched]] that so many people had come to celebrate him, and at one point his voice broke as he thanked everyone. What made it so special was seeing someone who rarely asks for anything finally being appreciated. Honestly, the whole thing was as rewarding for me as it was for him. There is a unique kind of happiness that comes from making someone else feel [[valued]]. It reminded me that thoughtful gestures often mean far more than expensive gifts. Seeing him so [[at peace]] that evening is a memory I will always [[treasure]], and it deepened our bond.

followUps.q: How does your father spend his time now that he has retired?
followUps.answer: He reads the newspaper for hours, visits his friends at the local tea stall and spends a lot of time in the village with my grandparents. He seems more relaxed than I have ever seen him.

followUps.q: Do you often do things to make your family happy?
followUps.answer: I try to. Usually it is small things, like bringing home sweets or taking my mother to visit her parents. I think those little gestures matter more than big occasions.
